summary: Defines fifteen metadata elements for describing resources across fields, known as the Dublin Core Metadata Element Set. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A short checklist of fifteen things to write on a label so you can describe anything, like title and author.

questions: what are the 15 dublin core elements
what are the dublin core elements
what is dublin core metadata used for
subtitle: Fifteen simple labels, such as title, creator and date, for describing almost any kind of resource.

tldr.problem: Electronic resources are hard to find unless they carry descriptions in a common vocabulary that works across fields such as libraries, research and publishing.
tldr.mechanism: The Dublin Core Metadata Element Set defines fifteen broad, generic elements (title, creator, subject, date and so on), each with a human label, a machine name, a definition and sometimes a usage comment.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Version 1.1 of the element set. It obsoletes RFC 2413, the first published version, and mainly rewords some definitions.

today: RFC 5013 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2413. No later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it.

sections.title: Where Dublin Core Came From
sections.content:
The Dublin Core Metadata Workshop Series began in 1995 with an invitational workshop that brought together librarians, digital library researchers, content experts and text-markup experts. The goal was to promote better discovery standards for electronic resources. The name comes from the workshop's location in Dublin, Ohio, and "core" reflects that the elements are broad and generic.

This RFC contains the text of Dublin Core Version 1.1, which is the basis of ANSI/NISO Z39.85-2001. Its text closely follows the 2007 revision of that standard.
sections.eli5: A group of librarians and computer people met in a town called Dublin and agreed on a simple way to label things so they are easy to find later.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
The element set is a standard for cross-domain resource description. A resource is anything that might be identified, the same definition used in RFC 3986 and in the DCMI Abstract Model, so the specification does not limit what can be described.

The elements are typically used inside an application profile, which constrains their use according to local or community requirements. Those implementation details are outside the scope of the RFC. The RFC also stays silent on whether elements may be repeated or appear in any order, because application profiles are the proper place for that.
sections.eli5: The checklist works for any thing at all, a book, a song or a picture. Each group that uses it can add its own house rules.

sections.title: How Elements Are Named
sections.content:
Each element has a descriptive label for people and a unique token, its name, for machine processing. Under the DCMI Namespace Policy, the name is appended to a DCMI namespace URI to build a globally unique identifier for the element. This RFC recommends lowercase element names, consistent with RDF property types.

The full set of DCMI vocabularies, called DCMI Metadata Terms, also includes a set of resource classes, the DCMI Type Vocabulary. Terms are meant to be combined with other compatible vocabularies on the basis of the DCMI Abstract Model.
sections.eli5: Every item on the checklist has a friendly name for people and a short code name for computers, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: The Fifteen Elements
sections.content:
The elements are title, creator, subject, description, publisher, contributor, date, type, format, identifier, source, language, relation, coverage and rights.

Some are about who was involved: creator is the entity primarily responsible for making the resource, contributor an entity responsible for contributions, and publisher an entity responsible for making it available. Each can be a person, an organization or a service. Others describe the thing itself: type is its nature or genre, while format is the file format, physical medium or dimensions such as size and duration.

Several elements recommend a controlled vocabulary as best practice: subject, type, format (for example Internet Media Types), language (for example RFC 4646) and coverage. For date, the RFC recommends an encoding scheme such as the W3CDTF profile of ISO 8601. For identifier, source and relation, it recommends a string from a formal identification system.
sections.eli5: The checklist asks things like what it is called, who made it, what it is about, when it was made, and what language it uses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the element set poses no risk to computers and networks. It poses minimal risk to searchers who obtain incorrect or private information through careless mapping from rich data descriptions to the Dublin Core elements. It states that no other security concerns are likely.
sections.eli5: A label cannot hurt a computer. The only risk is writing the wrong thing on the label or sharing something private by accident.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2413
sections.content:
RFC 2413 was the first published version of the Dublin Core (Version 1.0). The main differences are in wording: the definitions of contributor and date were semantically broadened, relation was clarified, and redundant references to "the content of" a resource were removed.

The RFC also recommends lowercase element names, drops statements on element ordering and repeatability, and points to the current abstract model, vocabularies and namespace policies. Changes to terms since 2001 have been reviewed by a DCMI Usage Board under the DCMI Namespace Policy.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the checklist. A few descriptions were reworded so they are clearer, but it still has fifteen items.
